title: Lester Young's tone and John Coltrane searching on the horn
summary: Dance says Lester's tone would not fill ballrooms without mikes; Caldwell found Coltrane always reaching for something.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: But (unintelligible) -- you know, when you -- you know, when you think back to all this business of tone and everything, well, I mean something that had to do with the fact that they were playing in these ballrooms where you wanted to produce a big sound.
I know, I mean -- whereas the kind of tone Lester had, if he wasn't miked, I mean you couldn't hear him.--
That's true. They had mikes (unintelligible) two big bandstands.
Well, what -- I mean what did you think of Lester when you first heard him?

Well, it was a peculiar style, and, you know, you always listen -- what the fellow's doing and what he's trying to do, like I never could fathom out what Coltrane wanted to do. I don't think he ever completed what he wanted to do.
Right. I've dug him -- when he used to come down to Small's and sit back up there and play, and seemed like he was always reaching for something or trying to

do something that he hadn't -- what he hadn't wanted -- what he hadn't accomplished. And I listened to him time and time again. And I talked with him. I liked things he did. He was always moving on his horn, but it seemed like the man was always like reaching for something.
It was also that, I think, what was -- when you heard those long things where he played for 15, 20 minutes, I mean it was an awful lot of repetition.
And I mean maybe you're just sort of, as you say, you're searching, but I mean a lot of that stuff really sounds like what you would do at home.
Where you're trying to work something out, but you don't do it in public or on a record.
